questions.question: Evaluate the socio-political causes and historical significance of the Kundara Proclamation (1809) in the trajectory of anti-colonial resistance in Kerala. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• The Kundara Proclamation of 1809 was issued by Velu Thampi Dalawa, the Diwan of
  • Travancore, against British interference in the affairs of the state.Causes:- British interference
  • in Travancore's administration and internal affairs- Opposition to the growing political
  • dominance of the East India Company- Economic pressure caused by financial obligations
  • and the Subsidiary Alliance- Conflict between Velu Thampi and the British Resident, Colonel
  • Macaulay- Desire to defend the sovereignty and independence of Travancore.Historical
  • significance:- called upon the people to unite against British authority- mobilised sections of
  • society against colonial domination- became an important episode in the early anti-colonial
  • resistance in Kerala- demonstrated the conflict between indigenous political authority and
  • British imperial expansion.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the main demands raised in the Malayali Memorial of 1891. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The Malayali Memorial, submitted to the Maharaja of Travancore in 1891, was a petition
  • demanding greater opportunities for educated Malayalis in government employment.Its major
  • demands were- Adequate representation of native Malayalis in government services-
  • Reduction of the dominance of non-Malayali Brahmins, particularly Tamil Brahmins, in
  • administrative positions- Equal employment opportunities for qualified Malayalis-
  • Recognition of the educational qualifications and abilities of local candidates- Fairness and
  • justice in public appointments.The memorial was signed by prominent individuals, including
  • K. P. Sankara Menon and Dr. Palpu, and received broad support from educated sections of
  • society. It marked an important stage in the development of political consciousness, organised
  • public action and demands for administrative representation in Travancore.

questions.question: What are the major features of coalition governments in Kerala? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Coalition governments are administrations formed by two or more political parties that
  • cooperate to secure a legislative majority. Major features - Bipolar political competition-
  • multi-party participation- Power sharing- Common programmes- Negotiation and
  • compromise- Role of smaller parties- Electoral accountability. Coalition politics has
  • encouraged pluralistic representation in Kerala, although it can also create disagreements
  • over leadership, policies and the distribution of power.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the contribution of land reforms to Kerala's social and economic development. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Land reforms were important in transforming Kerala's agrarian society by weakening
  • traditional landlordism and improving the position of cultivating tenants. Contributions: -
  • Abolition of tenancy exploitation- Security of tenure- Ownership rights- Reduction of social
  • inequality- Social empowerment- Rural transformation- Democratic participation.
  • Landlessness persisted among many agricultural labourers, particularly Dalit and Adivasi
  • communities, and the reforms did not eliminate all rural inequalities.Therefore, land reforms
  • were a major component of Kerala's social transformation, though their benefits were
  • unevenly distributed.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Describe the practices within Namboodiri society that V.T. Bhattathiripad criticised. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• V . T. Bhattathiripad was a prominent social reformer who challenged conservative
  • practices within Namboodiri Brahmin society.Hecriticised:- Eldest-son marriage privilege-
  • Restrictions on women's freedom- Child marriage- Restrictions on widow remarriage- Lack
  • of women's education- Caste hierarchy- Conservative customs. Through his writings, theatre
  • and reform activities, especially the play AdukkalayilNinnuArangathekkuhe advocated
  • women's emancipation and social reform.His contribution was significant in the development
  • of progressive thought within Kerala's Namboodiri community.

questions.question: Briefly explain the foundational features of Kerala's commercial and agricultural economy prior to European colonization. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Before European colonisation, Kerala had a flourishing agricultural and maritime
  • commercial economy. Majorfeatures: - Agricultural production- Spice cultivation -Maritime
  • trade- Port towns- Merchant communities- Agrarian social structure
  • - Regional and international exchange. Kerala's precolonial economy combined agriculture,
  • local markets and international maritime trade, laying the foundation for its later commercial
  • development.

questions.question: What were the major provisions of the Kerala Education Bill, 1957? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• The Kerala Education Bill was introduced by the first elected Communist government of
  • Kerala, led by E. M. S. Namboodiripad, in 1957. Education Minister Joseph Mundassery
  • played a major role in its formulation.Majorprovisions:- Regulation of private schools-
  • Teachers' service conditions- Salary protection- Appointment procedures- Educational
  • standards- Government supervision- Protection of teachers. The Bill generated strong
  • opposition from sections of private school managements and religious organisations,
  • contributing to the VimochanaSamaram (Liberation Struggle) of 1958–59.

questions.question: Explain the public health consequences associated with Endosulfan exposure in Kasaragod. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Endosulfan is a toxic organochlorine pesticide that was aerially sprayed over cashew
  • plantations in Kasaragod district, Kerala, for several years. Its use became the centre of a
  • major public health and environmental controversy.Public health consequences:-
  • Neurological problems: Exposed populations reported neurological disorders, including
  • seizures and developmental difficulties.- Congenital abnormalities: Some affected families
  • reported birth defects and developmental abnormalities.- Reproductive health concerns:
  • Reports included reproductive difficulties and other health problems.- Developmental
  • disorders: Children in affected areas experienced developmental delays and disabilities.-
  • Long-term health concerns: Persistent pesticide contamination raised concerns about
  • prolonged exposure through the environment.- Psychological and economic hardship:
  • Affected families faced emotional distress, medical expenses and caregiving burdens.-
  • Environmental contamination: Concerns arose over contamination of soil, water and local
  • ecosystems.The Endosulfan controversy led to public protests, demands for medical support
  • and compensation, and restrictions on the pesticide. Kerala prohibited its use, and India
  • subsequently banned it nationally in 2011.

questions.question: Analyse how Thrippadidanam served as a political tool for Marthanda Varma to neutralize internal rebellions by the Ettuveetil Pillamar and consolidate a fragmented feudal state into a centralized monarchy / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Thrippadidanam was a significant political and religious act performed by Marthanda
  • Varma in 1750, when he dedicated the Kingdom of Travancore to Lord Padmanabha of Sree
  • Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram.Thrippadidanam also served as a powerful
  • political instrument to legitimize royal authority, weaken rival power centres and consolidate
  • Travancore into a centralized monarchy- Before Marthanda Varma, Travancore was
  • characterized by the influence of powerful nobles, local chieftains and regional power
  • holders.- The EttuveetilPillamar, a group of eight influential noble families, traditionally
  • exercised considerable political and economic influence.- Marthanda Varma adopted military
  • and administrative measures to suppress the political influence of the EttuveetilPillamar and
  • other opponents.- Thrippadidanam strengthened this process by providing a religious and
  • ideological justification for the king's authority- The concept of Padmanabha Dasa gave his
  • rule a distinctive religious legitimacy- Thrippadidanam symbolically placed the entire
  • kingdom under the sovereignty of Lord Padmanabha, represented by the monarch.- It
  • reinforced the idea of a unified kingdom rather than a collection of territories controlled by
  • competing feudal authorities.- Marthanda Varma expanded royal control over administration,
  • revenue collection and military organization- The influence of local chieftains and hereditary
  • elites was reduced as the central government became more powerful- These developments
  • helped transform Travancore from a fragmented political order into a more centralized state-
  • The temple became a major symbol of Travancore's political identity and royal legitimacy-
  • Thus, it combined religious devotion with practical state-building.

questions.question: Examine Poykayil Appachan's narrations of slavery as a historical source for understanding Dalit oppression. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Poykayil Sree Kumara Gurudevan was a prominent Dalit social reformer, poet and anti-
  • caste thinker in Kerala. He founded the Prathyaksha Raksha Daiva Sabha (PRDS) in 1909 to
  • challenge caste discrimination and promote the dignity of oppressed communities. Through
  • his songs and narrations of slavery, he highlighted the historical suffering, exploitation and
  • social exclusion of Dalits in Kerala. Narrations of slavery as an alternative historical source-
  • PoykayilAppachan questioned conventional histories that neglected the experiences of
  • enslaved and oppressed communities. Exposure of the institution of slavery- His narrations
  • highlighted the existence of slavery in Kerala is subjected to caste-based exploitation- Social
  • discrimination and untouchability- Economic exploitation and landlessness- Recovery of
  • Dalit memory and identity- Critique of mainstream historiography- Resistance and social
  • emancipation- Historical significance and limitations-- His narrations provide valuable
  • insights into the experiences and collective memories of oppressed communities. His works
  • represent both a critique of caste society and an important contribution to Dalit-centred
  • historiography.

questions.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of coalition politics in Kerala. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Coalition politics refers to a political arrangement in which two or more political parties
  • come together to form a government or contest elections by sharing power and
  • responsibilities. Advantages of Coalition Politics in Kerala- Representation of diverse
  • interests- Strengthening of democracy- Political stability through established fronts-
  • Protection of minority interests- Promotion of consensus-based decision-making- Continuity
  • of welfare policies- Decentralisation of political power.Disadvantages- Political instability-
  • Compromise on ideological principles- Excessive bargaining by smaller parties- Delay in
  • decision-making- Compromise in policy implementation- Opportunistic alliances- Increased
  • political competition and factionalism- Limited accountability.

questions.question: Critically examine whether Kerala's land reform experience adequately addressed the land question of Dalit and Adivasi communities. / [CO4] [15x2 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Kerala's land reforms are considered an important achievement in India's social and
  • economic history. The Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, 1960, and the Kerala Land Reforms
  • Act, 1963, as amended in 1969, aimed to abolish tenancy, protect tenants and impose ceilings
  • on landholdings. These reforms weakened the traditional landlord system and improved the
  • social position of many agricultural tenants. -Achievements of land reforms-- Abolition of
  • tenancy- Reduction of landlord power - Social transformation - Political empowerment-
  • Improved living conditions. Limitations - Exclusion of agricultural labourers- Limited
  • redistribution- Continuing economic dependence - Historical caste inequalities- Unequal
  • distribution of benefits- Limitations concerning Adivasi communities-- Traditional land
  • alienation- Failure to recognise customary rights, their ancestral territories and forest
  • resources- Displacement and migration- Weak implementation of restoration measures-
  • Continuing land struggles. Kerala's land reforms achieved significant agrarian and social
  • transformation, but their benefits were unevenly distributed across caste and tribal
  • communities. [15x2 = 30]
